reference.source: Bradley and Daroff Neurology in Clinical Practice
clinicalPearls: Presents with progressive difficulty in word retrieval and impaired repetition of sentences and phrases, with slow, hesitant speech punctuated by word-finding pauses
Single-word comprehension and object knowledge are relatively preserved, distinguishing it from the semantic variant
Speech is not frankly agrammatic and there is no motor speech apraxia, distinguishing it from the non-fluent or agrammatic variant
The impaired repetition is thought to reflect a limitation of phonological short-term memory
The logopenic variant is most often underpinned by Alzheimer's disease pathology
Atrophy typically centres on the left temporoparietal junction and posterior superior temporal region
reference.pathophysiology: The logopenic variant of primary progressive aphasia arises from neurodegeneration of the left posterior temporal and inferior parietal cortex, regions important for phonological processing and verbal working memory. Impaired access to and maintenance of phonological representations produces the characteristic word-retrieval difficulty and the disproportionate impairment of sentence repetition. Unlike the other progressive aphasias, the logopenic syndrome is most commonly caused by underlying Alzheimer-type pathology rather than frontotemporal lobar degeneration.
additionalDifferentials: Non-fluent or agrammatic variant primary progressive aphasia
Anxiety or depression causing subjective word-finding complaints
additionalInvestigations: Comprehensive speech and language assessment characterising naming, repetition and comprehension
Neuropsychological evaluation of verbal working memory and other cognitive domains
MRI brain demonstrating left temporoparietal atrophy
Amyloid PET or CSF biomarkers to confirm or exclude Alzheimer pathology
Audiometry to exclude peripheral hearing loss contributing to communication difficulty
redFlags: Sudden onset or stepwise deterioration suggesting a vascular cause
Rapidly progressive aphasia raising concern for prion or inflammatory disease
Focal signs or headache suggesting a structural lesion
Early prominent behavioural change indicating an alternative degenerative syndrome
reference.prognosis: Logopenic variant primary progressive aphasia is progressive; language deteriorates over time and, because the underlying pathology is frequently Alzheimer's disease, more generalised cognitive decline commonly supervenes. Speech and language therapy and communication aids can support function, but there is currently no disease-modifying treatment for the aphasia itself.
pitfalls: Confusing the logopenic variant with the non-fluent variant because both feature effortful speech, despite the absence of agrammatism and apraxia
Attributing early symptoms to anxiety or normal ageing
Failing to pursue amyloid biomarkers, thereby missing treatable or trial-relevant Alzheimer pathology
references: Bradley and Daroff's Neurology in Clinical Practice, current edition
Gorno-Tempini et al., classification of primary progressive aphasia and its variants (Neurology)
management: Speech and language therapy targeting word-retrieval and sentence-repetition deficits, with communication strategies and augmentative aids as the mainstay
Confirmation of the underlying Alzheimer pathology with amyloid PET or cerebrospinal fluid biomarkers to guide treatment
Trial of a cholinesterase inhibitor such as donepezil, adding memantine as more generalised Alzheimer-type cognitive decline emerges
Consideration of amyloid-directed disease-modifying antibody therapy in confirmed, eligible Alzheimer pathology where available
Non-pharmacological management of mood and neuropsychiatric symptoms, with attention to swallowing, nutrition and safety as the disease progresses
Carer education, psychological support and timely advance care planning
Multidisciplinary follow-up through cognitive neurology services with monitoring of cognitive progression
